reasons: [reasoning_validity/major] D1 [CL2, CL5, criteriaAssessments C2 mechanisms, edgeCasesAndFailureModes[2], counterarguments[1], practicalImplications[0]] The draft gets the direction of the p99 summation error wrong. CL5, C2 mechanisms and edgeCasesAndFailureModes item 3 say summed per-hop p99s are 'an approximation, not a bound' and that correlated slowness can make end-to-end p99 'worse than the sum'. For positive latencies with independent hops, the p99 of the sum is normally below the sum of the p99s. Under perfect correlation the two are equal. So the sum is usually the conservative estimate. K7 (0.99^5 = 95.1% of requests avoid every hop's tail) measures how many requests hit at least one slow hop. It does not show the summed p99 is optimistic. This matters for the verdict. CL2 says sidecar mode 'fails R3' at 13 ms / 13.8 ms, but that rests only on summation, and the true end-to-end sidecar p99 could be materially lower, possibly near or under 10 ms. The counterargument response ('a plausible measurement error is unlikely to change the sidecar verdict') ignores this aggregation uncertainty. The sidecar failure should be stated as likely on a conservative sum, not as a finding. The end-to-end test should cover sidecar mode too, not only node-proxy.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [verdict; CL4; alternatives[2] ('Lattice node-proxy mode now'); K5, K6] The recommended option ('Lattice node-proxy mode now') does not include Portcullis this quarter. Yet its R3 headroom (5.3 ms total, 4.7 ms headroom, K5/K6) uses Portcullis's 0.8 ms datasheet edge figure. In the recommended configuration the edge would be Lattice ingress or some existing edge, and its latency is unknown (packet E7 limitations). The alternatives entry also quotes '4.5 to 5.3 ms', and the 4.5 ms lower end assumes zero edge cost, which CL11 itself says R3 does not allow. The verdict's '4.7 ms of headroom' is therefore attached to a configuration the draft is not recommending for this quarter. K10 (up to 5.5 ms of edge tolerated) is the correct framing for the recommended option and should replace the headroom figure there.

[decision_usefulness/major] D3 [verdict; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[4]; alternatives] The user asked which of TWO options to pick. The draft recommends a third configuration, conditional on two unconfirmed items: auditor acceptance and an end-to-end test. It gives no ranked fallback if the conditions fail or the strict either/or holds. In particular, it never says which product to adopt if the one-product limit is firm, R2 is needed this quarter, or node-proxy is rejected by the auditor. furtherResearch[4] only says this 'would force a choice between leaving R2 or R1 at risk' and does not make that choice. Given R1's hard audit date and R2's lack of a deadline, the draft has what it needs to state a fallback, but it does not.

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [verdict fallbacks (2) and (4); alternatives[4]; counterarguments[3]; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[5]] The new ranked fallbacks treat the Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE route inconsistently. Fallback (2), alternatives[4] and furtherResearch[5] call it 'the only single-product route in the packet that covers both R1 and R2'. But it needs a SPIRE deployment (a Workload API server the team must run, per E8) plus code changes in all 14 services. Calling it 'single-product' under a one-option-per-quarter limit is not justified, and the draft never checks whether SPIRE would count against that limit. Fallback (4) then drops the route: under the strict two-option framing it ranks Lattice over Portcullis because 'Portcullis alone fails the hard R1 requirement outright (E2)'. If Portcullis plus in-app mTLS counts as the Portcullis option in fallback (2), it should be compared with Lattice sidecar in fallback (4) too. It is not, and sidecar is itself likely to breach the hard R3 limit. Fallback (4) also recommends a configuration the draft expects to fail a hard requirement (CL2), and never says whether a likely R3 breach is better or worse than an R1 gap filled by in-app code. The fallback ladder needs one consistent definition of 'one option' and a direct comparison of sidecar against Portcullis plus go-spiffe in the strict case.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [criteriaAssessments C2 weaknesses[3]; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[0], [6]; verdict (K10 framing); CL4, CL11] The draft adds K12 ('with a 0.8 ms edge') and E19 (5 vs 6 segments) but never combines them, and it ties K12 to the Portcullis edge, which the recommended this-quarter setup does not include. I recomputed the numbers. With two node proxies per hop, the internal sum is 0.9 x 2 x 5 = 9.0 ms, so the unknown edge in the recommended setup (Lattice ingress or an existing edge) may add only 1.0 ms, not 5.5 ms (K10). Under the 6-segment reading with two proxies per hop, the internal sum is 0.9 x 2 x 6 = 10.8 ms, which breaks R3 with zero edge cost. With one proxy per hop and 6 segments, it is 5.4 ms, leaving 4.6 ms for the edge. So two ambiguities the draft lists separately can together reverse the node-proxy pass on the summed figure. The verdict's framing that the edge can add 'up to 5.5 ms' therefore overstates the headroom. This is the same kind of problem as prior D2, now appearing in changed material.

[minor/reviewer] D1 [criteriaAssessments C2 mechanisms; C2 weaknesses[3]; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[0]; K12-K14] New text in C2 mechanisms and the K12-K14 scenarios applies the 'two proxies per hop' doubling only to node-proxy mode. E5 (sources/internal-loadtest-2026-10.md) reports both modes in one 'Added p99 latency per hop' column. There are two ways to read that column. (i) It counts one proxy traversal. Then sidecar, which the draft itself says has proxies on both the client and server side of every hop, should be doubled as well, giving 2.6 x 2 x 5 = 26 ms. (ii) It counts one service-to-service hop. Then the node-proxy figure already includes both node proxies on a cross-node call, unless the test only measured same-node calls. The two-proxy node-proxy scenario is only coherent under a third reading: same-node test traffic against cross-node production traffic. The draft never states this reading. The pessimistic node-proxy figures (9.0 and 10.8 ms) are still worth raising, but the asymmetry should be explained. The sidecar conclusion does not change, because doubling only makes sidecar worse.
